mn2:1.2: On one occasion, the Buddha was staying in Sāvatthī, at Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
mn2:1.3: There, the Buddha addressed the monks:
mn2:2.1: “Monks, I will teach you the method for ending all taints.
mn2:2.2: Listen carefully and pay close attention; I will speak.”
mn2:3.1: “Monks, I declare the ending of taints for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know or see.
mn2:3.2: And what should one know and see to end the taints?
mn2:3.4: When one attends unwisely, unarisen taints arise, and arisen taints increase;
mn2:3.5: When one attends wisely, unarisen taints do not arise, and arisen taints are abandoned.
mn2:4.1: There are taints to be abandoned by seeing, by restraint, by using, by enduring, by avoiding, by removing, and by developing.
mn2:5.1: And what are the taints abandoned by seeing?
mn2:5.2: Here, an uninstructed ordinary person—who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and is untrained in the Dhamma of the noble ones—
mn2:5.3: does not understand what should be attended to and what should not be attended to.
mn2:5.4: Not understanding, they attend to what should not be attended to and do not attend to what should be attended to.
mn2:6.1: What should not be attended to?
mn2:6.2: When one attends to things that give rise to unarisen sensual taints, or increase arisen sensual taints;
mn2:6.3: unarisen taints of becoming, or increase arisen taints of becoming;
mn2:6.4: unarisen taints of ignorance, or increase arisen taints of ignorance—
mn2:6.5: these are things that should not be attended to.
mn2:6.7: When one attends to things that do not give rise to unarisen sensual taints, and abandon arisen sensual taints;
mn2:6.8: do not give rise to unarisen taints of becoming, and abandon arisen taints of becoming;
mn2:6.9: do not give rise to unarisen taints of ignorance, and abandon arisen taints of ignorance—
mn2:6.10: these are things that should be attended to.
mn2:7.1: When one attends unwisely, unarisen taints arise and arisen taints increase.
mn2:7.3: ‘Was I in the past? Was I not in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what was I in the past?’
mn2:7.4: ‘Will I be in the future? Will I not be in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? Having been what, what will I be in the future?’
mn2:7.5: Or they are inwardly confused about the present:
mn2:7.6: ‘Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? Where did this being come from? Where will it go?’
mn2:8.1: As they attend unwisely, one of six views arises:
mn2:8.5: or ‘I perceive self as not self,’
mn2:8.6: or ‘I perceive not self as self,’
mn2:8.8: ‘This self of mine speaks and feels, and experiences the results of good and bad actions; this self of mine is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever.’
mn2:8.9: This is called a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a distortion of views, a vacillation of views, a fetter of views.
mn2:8.10: Bound by the fetter of views, the uninstructed ordinary person is not freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and despair;
mn2:8.11: ‘They are not freed from suffering,’ I say.
mn2:9.2: who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and is trained in the Dhamma of the noble ones—
mn2:9.3: understands what should be attended to and what should not be attended to.
mn2:9.4: Understanding, they do not attend to what should not be attended to and attend to what should be attended to.
mn2:10.1: What should not be attended to?
mn2:10.2: When one attends to things that give rise to unarisen sensual taints, or increase arisen sensual taints;
mn2:10.3: unarisen taints of becoming, or increase arisen taints of becoming;
mn2:10.4: unarisen taints of ignorance, or increase arisen taints of ignorance—
mn2:10.5: these are things that should not be attended to.
mn2:10.7: When one attends to things that do not give rise to unarisen sensual taints, and abandon arisen sensual taints;
mn2:10.8: do not give rise to unarisen taints of becoming, and abandon arisen taints of becoming;
mn2:10.9: do not give rise to unarisen taints of ignorance, and abandon arisen taints of ignorance—
mn2:10.10: these are things that should be attended to.
mn2:11.1: When one does not attend to what should not be attended to and attends to what should be attended to, unarisen taints do not arise, and arisen taints are abandoned.
mn2:11.2: They attend wisely: ‘This is suffering,’ ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’
mn2:11.3: As they attend wisely, three fetters are abandoned:
mn2:11.4: identity view, doubt, and attachment to rules and rituals.
mn2:11.5: These are called the taints abandoned by seeing.
mn2:12.1: And what are the taints abandoned by restraint?
mn2:12.2: Here, a monk, with wise reflection, restrains the eye faculty.
mn2:12.3: If the eye faculty were unrestrained, taints of desire and distress might arise; but by restraining it, such taints do not arise.
mn2:12.9: If the mind faculty were unrestrained, taints of desire and distress might arise; but by restraining it, such taints do not arise.
mn2:12.10: If restraint were lacking, taints of desire and distress might arise; but by maintaining restraint, such taints do not arise.
mn2:12.11: These are called the taints abandoned by restraint.
mn2:13.1: And what are the taints abandoned by using?
mn2:13.2: Here, a monk uses robes with wise reflection:
mn2:13.3: only to ward off cold, heat, and the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles; and to cover their nakedness.
mn2:14.1: They use almsfood with wise reflection:
mn2:14.2: not for fun, indulgence, adornment, or decoration, but only to sustain this body, to avoid harm, and to support the holy life.
mn2:15.1: They use lodgings with wise reflection:
mn2:15.2: only to ward off cold, heat, and the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles; and for the enjoyment of seclusion.
mn2:16.1: They use medicines and supplies for the sick with wise reflection:
mn2:16.2: only to ward off painful feelings and for the sake of good health.
mn2:17.1: If they did not use these things wisely, taints of desire and distress might arise; but by using them wisely, such taints do not arise.
mn2:17.2: These are called the taints abandoned by using.
mn2:18.1: And what are the taints abandoned by enduring?
mn2:18.2: Here, a monk, with wise reflection, endures cold, heat, hunger, and thirst; the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles; harsh and malicious words; and bodily feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, unpleasant, and life-threatening.
mn2:18.3: If they did not endure these things, taints of desire and distress might arise; but by enduring them, such taints do not arise.
mn2:18.4: These are called the taints abandoned by enduring.
mn2:19.1: And what are the taints abandoned by avoiding?
mn2:19.2: Here, a monk, with wise reflection, avoids wild elephants, wild horses, wild bulls, wild dogs, snakes, stumps, thorns, pits, cliffs, and rough ground.
mn2:19.3: They avoid unsuitable seats, unsuitable places to walk, and bad friends. Wise companions in the holy life would suspect them of evil conduct if they were to frequent such places.
mn2:19.4: If they did not avoid these things, taints of desire and distress might arise; but by avoiding them, such taints do not arise.
mn2:19.5: These are called the taints abandoned by avoiding.
mn2:20.1: And what are the taints abandoned by removing?
mn2:20.2: Here, a monk, with wise reflection, does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought; they abandon, remove, and eliminate it. They do not tolerate an arisen thought of ill will… or an arisen thought of harming… or any other unwholesome, bad qualities that have arisen; they abandon, remove, and eliminate them.
mn2:20.3: If they did not remove these things, taints of desire and distress might arise; but by removing them, such taints do not arise.
mn2:20.4: These are called the taints abandoned by removing.
mn2:21.1: And what are the taints abandoned by developing?
mn2:21.2: Here, a monk, with wise reflection, develops the awakening factor of mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and ripens in release;
mn2:21.3: develops the awakening factor of investigation of principles…
mn2:21.8: equanimity, which is based on seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, and ripens in release.
mn2:21.9: If they did not develop these things, taints of desire and distress might arise; but by developing them, such taints do not arise.
mn2:21.10: These are called the taints abandoned by developing.
mn2:22.1: When a monk has abandoned the taints that should be abandoned by seeing, by restraint, by using, by enduring, by avoiding, by removing, and by developing;
mn2:22.2: they are called a monk who is restrained in all taints, who has cut off craving, untied the fetters, and, by fully understanding conceit, has made an end to suffering.
mn2:22.3: That is what the Buddha said.
mn2:22.4: The monks were delighted and rejoiced at his words.
mn2:22.5: The Discourse on All Taints is finished.
